processing: Ripe pu-erh blended from fermented material; one retailer describes a batch as an even blend of grade 5 leaf fermented the year before pressing.
harvest_season: Not tied to one picking: each batch blends tea fermented earlier.
appearance_dry: A tightly pressed 357 g brown cake, which one drinker found drier and more compact than another pu-erh.
appearance_liquor: Dense dark red-brown with a thick look.
appearance_wet: Soft dark brown leaf, smallish for a ripe blend if grade 5 predominates.
taste_profile: Drinkers describe a rich, smooth cup with chocolate, coffee and mushroom, and one noted a vanilla note at the back of the throat in later steeps.

brewing.notes: Rinse once and use near-boiling water. A fresh batch may still show some piling aroma, so let it air or rest first.

vintage_note: Sold by year and batch in 357 g cakes. A code such as 2301 means the first batch of 2023, and a retailer suggests resting that batch for a further six months to a year. Examples on sale range from 2008 to recent years.
description:
7452 is a Menghai Tea Factory ripe cake that retailers treat as a classic of the range, with a recipe they date to 1974. It uses a finer average leaf than the better-known grade 6 and 7 blends, at least by one retailer's description of grade 5.

The fermented tea is blended, then pressed firmly into a 357 g cake. Fresh batches can keep some piling smell, though a retailer notes that one batch had already mellowed by the time it was sold.

Drinkers talk about a thick, smooth cup with chocolate, coffee and mushroom, plus vanilla in later steeps for at least one of them. Near-boiling water and short early steeps keep it round rather than murky.

Buy by batch code and give a fresh cake some rest. It is also a fair choice for comparing with 7572 and 7262, to see what a difference in leaf grade does.
history:
Retailers date the 7452 line to 1974 and present it as a representative Menghai product. That date has not been confirmed in factory documents, and the wider history is clearer: Menghai was among the first factories to make ripe tea in 1973, and it took on the Dayi mark after privatisation in 1996.

Pressings on sale span at least 2008 to 2025.
